hook: The Norse explorer who reached America about 500 years before Columbus.

pages.x: Leif was born in Iceland around 970, the son of Erik the Red, a hot-tempered Norseman outlawed for killing. Erik sailed west and founded the first Norse settlement in Greenland in 985, giving it an attractive name to tempt settlers. Leif grew up on the family farm at Brattahlid.

In 999 Leif sailed to Norway, where King Olaf converted him to Christianity and sent him home to convert Greenland. On the way back he rescued shipwrecked sailors from a reef, and from then on was called Leif the Lucky. His mother built Greenland's first church.

A trader had sighted unknown land to the west. Around 1000 Leif bought his ship and sailed with 35 men. He found a land of flat rocks, then a wooded land, and farther south a mild country with salmon in the rivers and wild grapes, which he called Vinland, "wine land".

The saga says one of his crew, a German named Tyrker, went missing one evening. He came back excited, babbling in German and rolling his eyes. He had found vines and grapes, and so the land got its name.

For centuries many thought Vinland was just a story. Then in 1960 Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found the remains of Norse houses at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. Tree rings in wood cut there show the Norse were in America in the year 1021.
Leif Erikson was probably the first European to set foot in North America, nearly 500 years before Columbus. The settlement did not last, but the United States marks Leif Erikson Day every 9 October.
pts: Probably the first European in North America
Reached Vinland about 500 years before Columbus
